Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Vignette:
Hemi was sixty-three years old when he finally walked into the clinic, a thick-set man with calloused hands and a way of standing that kept his back to the nearest wall. He had been a construction worker for forty-two years, and for most of those years he had lived with a woman named Leilani, a woman whose love had arrived as a fist and stayed as a bruise. He could still picture the night it had finally ended: the way her hand had come down on the kitchen counter, palm flat, the sound like a board breaking. She had been yelling about something—he could not remember what—and then her hand was around his throat, and he had let himself go limp, the way he always did, because fighting back felt like admitting they were right to hit him. He had not fought back. He had waited until she let go, then he had gone to the garage and sat in the dark. She died of a stroke three years later, and for a while he had thought the terror would die with her. It did not.

In the months that followed, Hemi noticed that his own hands had become unbearable to look at. He would be gripping a steel beam on a scaffold, and the sight of his fingers—the same fingers she had once grabbed and twisted—would send a surge of heat through his chest, and he would have to look away. He avoided mirrors on the job site. When a coworker clapped him on the shoulder and asked about his weekend, Hemi would shrug and turn toward the exit sign, finding the red glow with his eyes before he could answer. Talking about the event was out of the question. He had come to believe that if he spoke the words aloud, the shame would solidify into something he could not carry.

His spending became a problem quietly. He started buying things he did not need—a new set of wrenches, a tilting saw, work boots he never wore—because the act of handing over cash or swiping his card gave him a minute of blankness, a moment when the memory did not press. His checking account dwindled, but he could not stop. The alternative was sitting alone in his apartment, where the silence asked him to think, and thinking led to the certainty that he was weak, that he could not trust himself to protect anyone, least of all himself. He felt dead inside, a hollow man walking through the motions.

At work, he became known as the man who stood near the roll-up door during safety meetings. He scanned every room for exits before he could hear what was being said. The foreman once joked that Hemi looked like he was planning a getaway, and Hemi had laughed, but the laugh had come out wrong. Ordinary sounds—a dropped hammer, a truck's air brake, a door slamming in the wind—made him jump so violently that other workers started stepping back from him. He began arriving at the job site early, not to prepare, but to survey the layout of the building and confirm that every doorway opened. At night, he woke at three or four in the morning, certain he had heard a footstep, and lay still in the dark, scanning the bedroom door until dawn.

He avoided conflict with a vigilance that felt like breath. When a younger worker challenged his measurement on a cut, Hemi said nothing and walked to the other end of the beam. He had learned long ago that disagreement could escalate into something physical, and his body remembered the lessons even if his mind tried to forget. He lost touch with the few friends Leilani had allowed him to keep, because their faces carried the shape of that old life. He could not see them without remembering the parties where she would smile and then punish him later for how he had danced.

What brought him to the clinic was the spending—his son had found the piles of unused tools in the garage and asked, gently, what was happening. Hemi had no answer. But when the son pressed, Hemi found himself talking about the hand on his throat, the look in her eyes that said he deserved it. His voice had cracked, and he had felt something stir in the hollow place. He was afraid of what might crawl out if he kept talking. He was more afraid of staying silent.
